about.title: San Marcos Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Work in San Marcos takes many shapes. Some people spend the day on construction sites off N Twin Oaks Valley Road, others stock shelves or run kitchens along W San Marcos Boulevard, and plenty drive for a living on SR-78 and S Rancho Santa Fe Road. When a shift ends in an injury, fault is usually not the first question. California workers' compensation generally covers you no matter who caused the accident, and it is normally the only claim you can bring against your own employer. If a subcontractor, a property owner, a defective machine, or another motorist played a role, though, a separate third-party injury claim may be available alongside comp. San Marcos logged 270 injury collisions in 2025, with 386 people hurt; for anyone driving as part of the job, a crash can raise both kinds of claims at once. We handle workplace injury and third-party claims and can help you understand which paths apply to you.

whyChoose.title: Why San Marcos Workers Choose Us

items.title: Comp is the floor, not always the ceiling
items.desc: Workers' compensation is usually the exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent third party can be held separately responsible. We will look for both.

items.title: Timelines that matter
items.desc: California asks you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, and third-party claims carry a two-year deadline. An early consultation helps make sure neither window closes on you.

items.title: Protection from pushback
items.desc: Retaliating against a worker for reporting an injury or filing a claim is illegal in California. We can address any pressure you feel from an employer while your claim moves forward.

items.question: I was rear-ended on SR-78 while making deliveries for my San Marcos employer. Is that a workers' comp case or a car accident case?
items.answer: It can be both. Because you were on the job, workers' compensation should cover your medical care and part of your lost wages regardless of fault. Separately, the driver who hit you is a third party, so you may also have a personal injury claim against that driver and their insurer, subject to California's two-year deadline.

items.question: What if I did not report my injury right away because I thought it was minor?
items.answer: California asks workers to notify their employer within 30 days of a job injury, so report it as soon as you realize it is a problem. A delay does not automatically end your rights, but it can complicate things. Put the report in writing and keep a copy, then talk with us about where you stand.

items.question: Do you charge me anything, and what happens next if I contact you?
items.answer: Your initial consultation is free, and there is no obligation to move forward. We handle personal injury matters on contingency, which means no fee unless there is a recovery. You decide whether to work with us.
